chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: Becoming music director; putting "Stompin' at the Savoy" forward
summary: McRae went through the book and pushed "Stompin' at the Savoy", which then went over big.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When I came back after the first tour with Chick, he decided to make me music director. You know, like, the fella that takes care of all the music and takes care of the -- you know, furnish him with ideas which he's supposed to do, you know. Work closely with him. Come up with some ideas that can make the band better and things like that.
And so, I began to go looking through the book, and I told Chick -- I said, "Stompin At The Savoy, why don't we play this?" So they played "Stompin At The Savoy" and

I liked it. I say, "Why don't you play it more often, this is a good number."
They had been playing "Stompin At The Savoy." But they had a lot of music. You must remember, Chick had a lot of arrangements that Sampson -- he had made "Stompin At The Savoy."
But he eventually made another arrangement on it and made it a little stronger since we started playing it a lot.
Now, before, he had a lot of other things, like "Blue Lou." Sampson wrote a lot of his tunes.
Sampson was a good writer. He's a good arranger, he's a good composer. He had the book there on a lot of Edgar Sampson things.
They were "Blue Lou" and a lot of other things and later things. He had made "Stompin At The Savoy" some time ago.
They probably had been playing it, you know. Because Sampson had made about eight or nine things in the book, you know.
